validator: draft 1 passes validate.mjs with no problems, soft points or warnings; the points below are the critic's.
keep: The idea is named up front (the same step triangle gives the distance along its long side and the midpoint halfway along it), and the first sentence of the method carries OpenStax's quote [1] on exactly those words: plot the points and draw the right triangle as for slope.
One fully worked example with numbers computed from the rule: A (1, 2), B (7, 10), √(36 + 64) = 10, and its midpoint (4, 6) both ways, by half the run and rise and by averaging.

The picture shows the cause, not just the effect, as the course brief asks: dragging B across both axes to (−5, −6) turns the differences negative but leaves 36 and 64, so the distance is still 10, and the reason (a negative times a negative is positive) is in the explanation.

Thirteen screens alternate SHOW and DO (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 show; 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 do) and end on two mixed puzzles (12, 13), the same shape as lesson 1. Each lesson 2 slip has a puzzle with its own hint: run plus rise (2, 4, 13), no square root (2, 13), dropped brackets (4), halving the differences instead of averaging (6, 8, 12), the lost minus (8) and working back wrongly (10).
The brief's 'not stated as common' midpoint slip (halving the difference) is taught as a check, not as a cited mistake.

Terms: two new ones, midpoint and distance formula; run, rise, gradient and hypotenuse are used as lesson 1 and Geometry fundamentals introduced them. Only three sources, each on words its quote supports; the ceiling plan and the tape are worded as examples.
fix: False absolute: 'Adding the run and the rise ... goes round the two short sides instead, which is always longer.' When the two points are level or one is straight above the other, one difference is 0 and the sum equals the distance. Say it is longer whenever the triangle has two sides, and give the check: the distance is no shorter than the larger difference and no longer than the two added.

Causal step skipped: the explanation says the midpoint is halfway along the run and halfway up the rise, but not why that point lands on the long side. Add the reason from lesson 1: a straight line climbs the same amount for each 1 along, so half the run along gives half the rise up.

Causal step skipped: 'Halfway between two numbers is their average' is asserted. Show it from the numbers: 1 plus half of 7 − 1 is 1 + 3 = 4, and (1 + 7) ÷ 2 is 4 too, because adding half the gap to the smaller number lands where halving the total does.

A condition the result needs is missing: the distance is a real length only when a square across and a square up stand for the same length, as on a plan drawn in metres both ways. Lesson 1 taught graphs whose axes carry different units (volts against amps), and lessons 5 and 6 go back to them, so the dossier must say the long side of such a graph is not a length. It goes in explain and practice, not ignores, since the result depends on it.

Practice does not stand on its own: working back from a midpoint is in explain and screen 10 but not in practice, and the brackets slip, taught on screen 4, is missing from its mistakes. Add a working-back step with an example, the brackets mistake, the wrong working back (the midpoint of the end and the midpoint), and the size check.
The worked example in practice stops at the midpoint. Check it as the screens do: from (−2, 7) to (1, 3) is 3 along and 4 down, half the run and half the rise.
The analogy's numbers (1.2 m, 4.8 m, 3 m, 3.6 m) are not in numbers. List them as assumed and computed.
